summary: A 1976 recommendation for a host-to-host protocol for a network that would use ARPANET IMPs without change but allow the upper-level protocols to be redone. It is a lightly edited planning document shared with the community.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone was designing a new network using the same routers but wanted new rules for computers talking. This note shares that plan.

questions: host to host protocol arpanet type network
subtitle: A redesigned host-to-host protocol for ARPANET-like networks

tldr.problem: The ARPANET Host-to-Host Protocol had limitations: it required separate connections in each direction (simplex), could not recover from certain message losses, wasted bandwidth on flow control by using a reverse channel instead of piggybacking, and made it cumbersome to establish communication with service facilities.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes a full-duplex host-to-host protocol using sequence numbers and a sliding window for flow control. Connections carry traffic in both directions, flow control information travels on the reverse channel when available, and the protocol gracefully recovers from lost messages by requiring each message to identify itself.
tldr.outcome: The protocol design was comprehensive but not adopted by ARPANET. It demonstrated thinking about alternatives and influenced later protocol designs. The trade-offs between efficiency and generality shaped subsequent network architecture.

today: RFC 714 is a thoughtful redesign of the ARPANET Host-to-Host Protocol. Although it was not adopted, it demonstrated the design space of host protocols and the trade-offs between efficiency and robustness. Its concepts influenced later protocol design thinking.

sections.title: Limitations of the Current Protocol
sections.content:
The ARPANET Host-to-Host Protocol (NCP), in use since 1972, was the first protocol for a packet-switched network. It remained adequate for its job, but had known deficiencies. Most significantly, it treated connections as simplex (one direction), forcing two connections to carry a bidirectional exchange. It was not robust in the face of message loss. It wasted bandwidth on flow control by requiring a separate channel to convey flow control information rather than piggybacking it on reverse traffic. It made establishing communication with service facilities cumbersome.

RFC 714 presents an alternative protocol that addresses these issues, borrowing from the IFIP (International Federation for Information Processing) end-to-end protocol while optimizing for a single autonomous network with short delays and reliable delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way had to set up two separate connections back and forth. The new way uses one connection both ways, and when someone says 'I am ready for more data,' they say it on the way back instead of needing a separate message.

sections.title: Full-Duplex Connections and Windowing
sections.content:
The proposed protocol treats connections as full-duplex entities carrying traffic in both directions. Instead of acknowledging each message individually, it uses a sliding window for flow control inspired by the IFIP protocol but simplified for ARPANET-like networks. When a connection is established, sequence numbers initialize and the receiver allocates a window of credits (permissions to send). A sender can transmit as many messages as would fit within the window.

When the receiver gets messages at the left edge of the window, it acknowledges the rightmost such message and advances the window. It sends back acknowledgements and new credits, which can be piggybacked on traffic flowing in the reverse direction. For recovery, if a sender does not receive an acknowledgement within a timeout, it retransmits with the same sequence number, allowing the receiver to detect and discard duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of 'message 1 received' and 'send more', the new way says 'I am ready for messages 1 through 8.' When messages arrive, it updates: 'now I am ready for 9 through 16.' This lets one connection do what the old way needed two for.

sections.title: Connection Management and Addressing
sections.content:
A Network Control Program (NCP) in each host manages connections on behalf of processes. The protocol uses a standard name space of sockets (identified by host number and a 16-bit socket number) as connection endpoints. Since transmitting a full 32-bit socket pair in every message would be wasteful, connection establishment allows each host to map the socket pair to a short index.

Connection establishment uses an RFC (request for connection) command that specifies both socket addresses, an index for data messages, a maximum message size, and initial credit. The connection is confirmed when both sides exchange matching RFCs. Termination uses a CLS (close) command; both sides must send and receive one before the socket pair is released for reuse. The protocol gracefully handles message loss by allowing retransmission and duplicate detection.
sections.plainLanguage: Sockets are like phone numbers for different programs. To call, you say 'I am at phone 123 calling 456,' and they say back 'OK, I am at 456 calling you at 123,' and you have a connection. When done, both say goodbye before hanging up.
